name: Buckwheat
label: buckwheat cover

planting.note: Broadcast ~1–1½ oz over the whole 32 sq ft bed (2–3 lb per 1,000 sq ft, Johnny's green-manure rate) and rake in ½–1 in. Sow from after last frost until ~4–6 weeks before first frost.

bed30.note: drill 1–2 seeds per inch in rows 4–6 in apart (Johnny's), or broadcast and rake — the rows are just drill lines

watch_for: Not frost tolerant at all — the first real frost kills it (use that). Mow within 7–10 days of the first flowers or seed sets, hardens and falls, and you get buckwheat volunteers (SARE, UMaine). It regrows if cut before ~25% bloom, so wait for full flower if you want it dead.
watering: Water once to germinate; after that it's on its own — it wilts in drought but bounces back overnight.
method_notes: The summer gap-filler, not a legume: it scavenges phosphorus (SARE: nearly 3x barley, >10x rye) and blankets weeds in 2–3 weeks, flowering in 4–6 weeks (MOFGA). Terminate at first flower — 30–45 days from sowing — turning in soft residue that breaks down in days; Coleman sows it through the frost-free period, ending 4 weeks before first frost (The Self-Fed Farm and Garden, ch. 6). Follow with a fall crop or fall cover immediately: it leaves soil loose and the released P can leach (SARE). It fixes no nitrogen, so plant it to catch nutrients for a hungry crop — but don't expect it to feed one. No same-family restriction for common vegetables; nothing botanical to avoid after it, only idle bare soil.
source: UMaine Extension Soil Testing Lab 'Selected Green Manures and Cover Crops for Maine'; UMaine Bulletin #2270 (Maine Forage Facts: Small Grains); MOFGA 'Using Green Manures' (E. Sideman); SARE Managing Cover Crops Profitably 3rd ed., Buckwheat chapter; Johnny's Buckwheat Cover Crop key growing info; Fedco Farm Seed at a Glance; Eliot Coleman, The Self-Fed Farm and Garden, ch. 6 (sowing window, per Sustainable Market Farming review).

name: Crimson clover
label: crimson clover cover

planting.note: Broadcast ~¼ oz over the whole 32 sq ft bed (⅓–½ lb per 1,000 sq ft, Johnny's) or up to ¾ lb per 1,000 (UMaine), ½ in deep. Sow spring to early summer for a same-season green manure; sow by early–mid September to try to overwinter.

bed30.note: broadcast and rake in ½ in deep (UMaine) — rows are just drill lines

watch_for: Winterkill in an open Maine winter — UMaine rates it 'not hardy in Northern New England', Johnny's says it only occasionally survives parts of Zone 5 with snow cover. Sown too early in fall it flowers before winter and dies. If it survives and you let pods mature, it volunteers. Deer browse it.
watering: Water to establish the stand; once rooted it needs nothing until you mow it.
method_notes: A legume, but in Northern New England treat it as a spring annual (UMaine): spring-sown it fixes ~50–60 lb N/A (MOFGA; SARE measured >50 lb N/A in zone 5b/6a trials) and reaches flowering in 70–90 days — mow at full bloom for the most nitrogen and the cleanest kill (SARE: full bloom kills it completely). Two honest Maine uses: sow spring to early summer and turn in by midsummer for a heavy feeder, or sow late summer as a winter-killed annual — it 'occasionally survives in parts of Zone 5 with adequate snow cover' (Johnny's), and if it doesn't survive you get easy-to-manage residue in spring (SARE). Don't follow it with other Fabaceae — beans, peas, more clover; and give 2–3 weeks before direct-seeding small seeds: crimson residue can slow germination of onion, carrot and tomato (SARE lab work).
source: UMaine Extension Soil Testing Lab 'Selected Green Manures and Cover Crops for Maine' (crimson clover: spring annual, not hardy in Northern New England, 20–30 lb/A); MOFGA 'Using Green Manures' (70–90 days to flowering, 50–60 lb N/A); Johnny's Clovers & Alfalfa key growing info (⅓–½ lb per 1,000 sq ft; Zone 5 occasional survival with snow); SARE Managing Cover Crops Profitably 3rd ed., Crimson Clover chapter.

name: Winter rye
label: winter rye cover

planting.note: Broadcast ~1–1½ oz over the whole 32 sq ft bed (2–3 lb per 1,000 sq ft, Johnny's; UMaine 2 lb) and rake in ~1 in. Sow mid-August to early October in zone 5 — the latest-plantable cover of all (UNH); late sowings need ~2x seed (MOFGA, Fedco).

bed30.note: broadcast and rake in 1 in deep, or drill — rows are just drill lines

watch_for: The spring escape: kill before stems elongate (UNH) — before seed heads in early to mid-May in Maine — or volunteer rye weeds your beds all summer. Late-killed rye gets woody and ties up nitrogen (SARE). Allelopathic residue can slow the next crop; wait 1–2 weeks after turning in (MOFGA). Avoid poorly drained spots (UMaine).
watering: Water to germinate if the fall is dry; after that, never — rye's whole job is growing where nothing else will.
method_notes: The scavenger and the organic-matter workhorse: the hardiest cereal, seeded later than any other cover, and the best net for leftover nitrogen — it holds 25–50 lb N/A over winter, up to 100 (SARE). This is Coleman's bulk-OM crop: rye with vetch over winter, turned under and allowed to decompose ~3 weeks before planting (The Self-Fed Farm and Garden; 'if he needs bulk organic matter, he grows rye and vetch' — Joe Gardener ep. 448). Sown mid-August to early October (UNH: even early October in southern NH), killed early the following spring — before stem elongation, ~early–mid May in Maine (UNH). Count on a short N tie-up right after incorporation (high C:N) and pair it with a legume (vetch at ~1 lb per 1,000 sq ft; Johnny's 70 lb/A rye + 30 lb/A vetch) or follow with a heavy feeder. Not a legume — it feeds nothing by itself. Don't follow it with wheat or barley: volunteer rye contaminates a small-grain stand (SARE).
source: UMaine Extension Soil Testing Lab green-manure chart (90 lb/A, seed into late September, must be killed); UMaine Bulletin #2270; MOFGA 'Using Green Manures' (90–150 lb/A, mid-Aug to late Sept, mid-Oct in warm Maine spots, allelopathy wait); UNH Extension 'Cover Cropping for the Home Garden' (2022); Johnny's How to Grow Winter Rye (zone 5: mid-Aug to mid-Oct, 2–3 lb per 1,000 sq ft); SARE Managing Cover Crops Profitably 3rd ed., Cereal Rye chapter; Fedco Farm Seed at a Glance; Eliot Coleman, The Self-Fed Farm and Garden (rye+vetch over-winter).

name: Hairy vetch
label: hairy vetch cover

planting.note: Broadcast ~½–¾ oz over the whole 32 sq ft bed (1–1½ lb per 1,000 sq ft, UMaine; Johnny's 1 lb) and rake in 1 in. Sow mid-August to September 15 (UNH) — it needs 30–40 days of growth before a killing frost (Johnny's). Inoculate with pea/vetch inoculant.

bed30.note: broadcast and rake in 1 in deep, or drill (Johnny's); for support add ~1 oz winter rye (1 lb vetch + 2–3 lb rye per 1,000 sq ft)

watch_for: Hard seed: any pods that mature mean vetch volunteers for years (SARE, NC State). Sensitive to frost heaving on bare ground (UMaine) — sow by mid-September or lose the stand. Kill it before bloom and you throw away most of the nitrogen. Slow fall growth means weeds can win if it's sown late.
watering: Water to establish the fall stand; spring growth needs nothing.
method_notes: The nitrogen engine of the rotation: fixes 60–150 lb N/A (MOFGA; Fedco lists ~100) — enough for corn, squash, tomatoes, brassicas. But it earns it slowly: sow mid-August to September 15 (UNH) so roots hold against frost heave, it crawls and vines through winter, then in spring wait for full bloom (mid-to-late May in Maine) — MOFGA: don't kill it until it flowers; NC State/SARE: ~50% bloom balances maximum N with easy incorporation. Mow to kill; tillage alone on viny growth is miserable, so mow first (Johnny's). Coleman partners it with rye (~4:1) for vine support and easier cutting; the rye offsets its own N tie-up with the vetch's N. Don't follow it with another legume — you've already made the nitrogen it would make.
source: UMaine Extension Soil Testing Lab green-manure chart (1–1½ lb per 1,000 sq ft, 1 in deep, rye support at 56 lb/A, frost-heave caution); MOFGA 'Using Green Manures' (20–40 lb/A, sow mid-Aug, 60–150 lb N/A, kill at flower); UNH Extension 'Cover Cropping for the Home Garden' (sow by Sept 15); Johnny's Hairy Vetch key growing info (1 lb per 1,000 sq ft, 30–40 days before killing frost, 20–25 lb/A vetch + 70 lb/A rye); SARE Managing Cover Crops Profitably 3rd ed., Hairy Vetch chapter; NC State Organic Commodities (terminate ~50% bloom); Fedco Farm Seed at a Glance.

name: Field peas and oats
label: peas & oats cover

planting.note: Broadcast ~2½ oz of the mix over the whole 32 sq ft bed (5 lb per 1,000 sq ft, Fedco/Johnny's) and rake in ~1 in. Spring: sow as soon as the soil works. Fall: sow Aug 15–Sept 7 to winterkill (Coleman). Inoculate the peas.

bed30.note: broadcast and rake in; peas really want 1½–3 in deep (Johnny's), so rake well — rows are just drill lines

watch_for: Spring-sown: mow at pea full bloom before the oats head out, or the woody oats are miserable to turn in (UMaine: 'can be difficult to incorporate') and the hollow pea stems won't mow cleanly after bloom (SARE). Fall-sown peas can survive a mild coastal winter — be ready to mow survivors. The dead oat mat keeps soil cold in spring (MOFGA); rake it aside for early crops.
watering: Moisture at sowing for even germination — pea seed must not dry out — then nothing until termination.
method_notes: The quick legume-plus-grass mix: peas fix nitrogen (90–150 lb N/A for field peas, SARE), oats scaffold the climbing peas, add biomass, scavenge leftover N, and — the point in Maine — both winterkill (UMaine PVO: not winterhardy; Johnny's: 'not frost-tolerant, a good option for a winterkilled cover crop'). Spring use: sow as soon as the soil works, mow at pea bloom before oats head, ~60–90 days (Fedco). Fall use, Coleman's Maine schedule: sow August 15–September 7, winter kills it, and rake the dead mat aside in spring to plant early crops without tilling ('winter-killed green manures... can sometimes be raked aside', The Self-Fed Farm and Garden, ch. 6). Peas are Fabaceae: don't follow with beans or peas. Mow before oats set grain or you'll be weeding volunteer oats; residue is low C:N and breaks down fast — good before anything except another legume.
source: UMaine Extension Soil Testing Lab green-manure chart (pea-vetch-oats mix 150/30/50 lb/A, not winterhardy, difficult to incorporate); UMaine Bulletin #2270 (oats 40–60 lb/A cover, 30–40 days before first frost, will not survive winter); Fedco Pea/Oat Mix (5 lb per 1,000 sq ft, 150–200 lb/A, spring–late summer); Johnny's Field Pea and Oats key growing info (pea 5 lb per 1,000 sq ft alone, 3 lb in a mix; oats 4 lb per 1,000 sq ft; sow early–mid spring or late summer/early fall); SARE Managing Cover Crops Profitably 3rd ed., Field Peas and Oats chapters; MOFGA 'Using Green Manures'; Eliot Coleman, The Self-Fed Farm and Garden, ch. 6 (sow Aug 15–Sept 7 to winterkill, per Sustainable Market Farming review).
